questions.q: What does this lesson explicitly say about its own content?
options: It is an orientation to the shape of a few regulations, not legal advice or a comprehensive survey
It is a complete and sufficient substitute for legal counsel
It covers every data privacy regulation in the world
It guarantees compliance for any organization that follows it
questions.explain: The lesson states plainly that real compliance obligations require actual legal counsel, not a foundations course.

questions.q: Which of these best describes GDPR's scope and consent model?
options: Applies globally to processing EU residents' personal data; generally requires opt-in consent
Applies only to California residents; uses an opt-out model
Applies only to US healthcare providers
Has no consent requirements of any kind
questions.explain: GDPR applies based on whose data is processed (EU residents), regardless of where the processing organization is based, and generally requires opt-in consent.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between GDPR and CCPA's consent models, per this lesson?
options: GDPR generally defaults to opt-in consent; CCPA generally defaults to opt-out for sale/sharing
They use the exact same consent model with no differences
GDPR has no consent requirements while CCPA requires consent for everything
CCPA only applies to companies outside the United States
questions.explain: This is the lesson's single most important takeaway: GDPR requires consent before processing; CCPA collects by default and expects the consumer to opt out.

questions.q: What does HIPAA specifically protect, and who does it apply to?
options: Protected Health Information (PHI), applying to covered entities and their business associates in US healthcare contexts
All personal data worldwide, for any type of business
Only financial transaction data
Only data belonging to European Union residents
questions.explain: Unlike GDPR and CCPA's broader personal-data scope, HIPAA is specific to PHI within US healthcare covered entities and business associates.

questions.q: Why does this lesson connect regulation back to Chapter 4's earlier lessons on policy?
options: Because regulatory requirements are often the real reason a policy exists and a common trigger for revising it during its lifecycle
Because regulations and policies have no real connection to each other
Because every company's policies are legally required to be identical
Because regulation only matters after a policy has already been retired
questions.explain: A policy like 'customer financial data is confidential' is often a direct translation of a regulatory obligation, and new or changed regulation is a common lifecycle trigger (Lesson 22).
